items.title: validateHttp() Has No Async Machinery: A Trace From Signal Forms Down to fetch() 🔍🚀
items.summary: Let's be honest: async validation is the part of any forms library where you brace yourself. Debouncing, cancelling the request the user just invalidated by typing another character, keeping a "checking..." spinner honest, not letting a slow response overwrite a fast one. Every library that has ever done this has grown a pile of bespoke machinery for it. So when Signal Forms shipped validateHttp() and it just worked, I wanted to see the pile. I opened the source expecting a few hundred lines of async bookkeeping, and instead found a function whose entire body is a single call to something else. That turned into a trace all the way down, from a form field to the line where bytes actually leave the browser. Six layers, and only two of them add anything you could call new async machinery. ✅ Availability: validateHttp() is @publicApi 22.0 , stable. Every source reference in this article is pinned to the v22.1.1 tag , so the line numbers stay valid even as main moves. 🧩 The View From Outside The usage is unremarkable, which is the point. You declare that a field validates against an endpoint, and you're done: const schema = form ( this . model , ( path ) => { validateHttp ( path . username , { request : ({ value }) => `/api/username-available?u= ${ value ()} ` , debounce : 300 , onError : () => ({ kind : ' server-unreachable ' }), onSuccess : ( res : { available : boolean }) => res . available ? undefined : { kind : ' username-taken ' }, }); }); Sync validators run first, the request waits until they pass, field().pending() is true while it's in flight, and typing again cancels the previous call. If you've read Part 3 of my Signal Forms series , that's the behaviour contract you already know. The question here is who implements it. 🔍 Layer 1: validateHttp() Is a Delegation Here is the whole function, from validate_http.ts : export function validateHttp ( path , opts ) { validateAsync ( path , { params : opts . request , debounce : opts . debounce , factory : ( request ) => httpResource ( request , opts . options ), onSuccess : opts . onSuccess , onError : opts . onError , when : opts . when , }); } That's it. No await, no subscription, no cancellation logic. The URL function you wrote becomes the params of something, and httpResource() gets handed over as a factory . Out of the whole file, that factory is the only line that does anything HTTP-related; everything else naming HTTP is an import, a type or a doc comment. So the async machinery is in validateAsync . Let's go there. 🧠 Layer 2: Three Behaviours, Zero New Mechanisms validate_async.ts is where I expected the pile to be. It isn't there either. Three behaviours, each one built from something that already existed. Sync-before-async gating is just returning undefined . The computation that feeds the resource's params does this: if ( validationState . shouldSkipValidation () || ! validationState . syncValid ()) { return undefined ; } A resource() whose params computation returns undefined sits in idle and never calls its loader — loadEffect() returns early as soon as it sees extRequest.request === undefined . That's documented public behaviour, not a forms detail. The docs promise that async validation runs only after all synchronous validation passes. Nobody implemented that promise here. It falls out of a rule that was already there. pending() is a resource status, read through a validator. The async error rule is a switch (lightly condensed here — the real one wraps each result in addDefaultField() to attach it to the field): switch ( res . status ()) { case ' idle ' : return undefined ; case ' loading ' : case ' reloading ' : return ' pending ' ; case ' resolved ' : case ' local ' : return res . hasValue () ? opts . onSuccess ( res . value () ! , ctx ) : undefined ; case ' error ' : return opts . onError ( res . error (), ctx ); } Six resource statuses collapse into four form outcomes. field().pending() holds no state of its own, it's a projection of res.status() . Debounce composes two existing primitives instead of writing a timer: if ( opts . debounce !== undefined ) { const debouncedResource = debounced (() => params (), opts . debounce ); const wrappedParams = computed (() => ɵchain ( debouncedResource )); return opts . factory ( wrappedParams ); } debounced() is a public (still experimental) @angular/core primitive, and ɵchain is the internal side of ctx.chain() , the resource-composition helper you reach through a params context. The file does declare export function chain() , but it carries no @publicApi marker and is not surfaced on @angular/core 's public entry point, which is why the forms code reaches it through the ɵ -prefixed alias rather than importing it by name. The forms team is chaining a debounced resource into a loader's params exactly the way you would chain any two resources in your own code. Worth noticing that they're dogfooding an experimental API in a stable feature. ⚙️ Layer 3: httpResource() Swaps the Loader httpResource() extends ResourceImpl and doesn't override any of the loading logic. It passes in a loader that subscribes to HttpClient , and it adds three signals: Signal What it is Resets on request change? progress linkedSignal sourced from extRequest Yes, by the graph statusCode linkedSignal sourced from extRequest Yes, by the graph headers computed over a linkedSignal , gated on status Yes, plus stays undefined until resolved / error So changing the request resets all three with no reset code involved — and the gate on headers means you never read half-populated headers mid-flight. The one place a reset is written by hand is override set() , which clears all three when you write a value locally. The signal graph covers the request path; the local-write path doesn't go through it. One line inside that loader is the bridge between the signal world and the HTTP world: sub = this . client . request ( request ! ). subscribe ({ /* ... */ }); 🔧 Layer 4: The Pipeline Everything Shares ResourceImpl is the actual engine, and it's four reactive nodes. The one I'd single out is the state machine, because it explains a UI behaviour you've probably relied on without asking why: // the branch taken when the resource already has previous state status = request === undefined ? ' idle ' : ' loading ' ; There are two of these, one per branch of an if / else inside that linkedSignal . The first covers initialisation and can also resolve straight from an initial stream; the second is the one above, taken when params change on a resource that already exists. Both send undefined to 'idle' . That expression runs inside a linkedSignal , which means it's not behind an await . linkedSignal is lazy, it recomputes on read rather than on write, but that recomputation is pure and synchronous: the first read of status() after your params change already returns 'loading' , and pending() is already true, in the same tick, before any promise exists. Only the data is async. If you've ever wondered why Signal Forms' pending state doesn't flicker, that's the reason: the state transition doesn't live inside the async function. The loader itself is called by exactly one effect whose only tracked dependency is the request. Nobody calls the loader imperatively. The graph decides that work should happen, and a single effect does it. It's the same lazy, pull-based model I traced in Internals #1 , which is a good sign: you learn this machine once and it keeps showing up. 🔌 Layer 5: Where the Trace Goes Dark Follow client.request(...) downward and you hit a wall. HttpClient hands off to HttpHandler , HttpHandler hands off to HttpBackend , and both of those are abstract classes with a single handle() method and no implementation. Grep as hard as you like, no import leads to the code that touches the network. That's because the binding isn't an import, it's a provider. From provider.ts , reformatted here to fit the width (the real HttpBackend entry uses a block-bodied factory, and each object sits on its own lines): const providers : Provider [] = [ HttpClient , FetchBackend , HttpInterceptorHandler , { provide : HttpHandler , useExisting : HttpInterceptorHandler }, { provide : HttpBackend , useFactory : () => inject ( FetchBackend )}, { provide : HTTP_INTERCEPTOR_FNS , useValue : xsrfInterceptorFn , multi : true }, ]; provideHttpClient() is the only place in the framework where those two abstract tokens get a concrete answer. Two details are easy to get wrong here. First, HttpClient itself is @Injectable({providedIn: 'root'}) and FetchBackend is auto-provided too, so both classes are reachable from a bare injector. Forgetting provideHttpClient() doesn't fail on HttpClient , it fails with No provider for HttpHandler , because the class resolves and its dependency doesn't. Second, re-listing HttpClient and the backends in that array isn't redundant. It re-provides them at the environment injector where you called the function. That's what lets a lazy route have its own interceptors, instead of everything collapsing onto one root instance. This is also why swapping the transport is a one-line change: Feature What it adds Status at v22.1.1 withFetch() {provide: HttpBackend, useExisting: FetchBackend} Deprecated — " FetchBackend is the default HttpBackend " withXhr() {provide: HttpBackend, useExisting: HttpXhrBackend} Supported — still needed for upload progress and JSONP 🌐 Layer 6: The Floor FetchBackend is where Angular stops and the platform starts: private readonly fetchImpl = inject ( FetchFactory , { optional : true })?. fetch ?? ((... args ) => globalThis . fetch (... args )); const fetchPromise = this . ngZone . runOutsideAngular (() => this . fetchImpl ( request . urlWithParams , { signal , ... init }), ); Even the last hop is injectable. And notice handle() returns new Observable(...) , so nothing was sent until layer 3 called .subscribe() . The cold Observable is the hinge the whole chain turns on: the resource's effect decides when, and the subscription is the trigger. Cancellation runs back up the same path in reverse. Typing another character changes the params signal, so the effect aborts its AbortController , the httpResource loader unsubscribes, the RxJS teardown aborts a second AbortController inside FetchBackend , and that one is the signal handed to fetch . Four different cancellation idioms relayed in sequence, with a staleness check at the top that rejects a late response by object identity in case anything slips through. ✅ Closing Thoughts Lined up, the whole stack is one pipeline with one part swapped at each level: Layer What it swaps What it adds validateHttp() The params Nothing at all — the body is one delegating call validateAsync() The params again, now gated and debounced The translation from resource status into form errors httpResource() The loader headers() , statusCode() , progress() ResourceImpl Nothing — it is the pipeline Status, cancellation, staleness HttpClient The transport, through DI Interceptors, XSRF, the transfer cache FetchBackend Nothing either — it's the floor Chunked body reading, progress, timeouts, and finally globalThis.fetch FetchBackend is the one row worth a caveat: there is real code down there, it just isn't async validation code. None of the debouncing, cancelling or pending-state logic we came looking for lives below ResourceImpl . The reason this matters beyond trivia: there's no forms-specific async system to learn, work around, or wait on the team to extend. If you understand resource() , you already understand validateHttp() , and anything it does you can reproduce with public APIs. Gate a loader by returning undefined . Render pending state off status() . Debounce by chaining a debounced() resource into your params. That's the entire feature. It's also a fair signal about the abstraction's honesty. A thin layer over primitives you can reach yourself is one you can debug at 6pm on a Friday, and one that inherits every improvement made underneath it for free. If you want to walk it yourself, clone the repo at v22.1.1 and read in this order: validate_http.ts , validate_async.ts , common/http/src/resource.ts , then core/src/resource/resource.ts (the constructor, then loadEffect ). A nice runtime check: provide a custom FetchFactory that logs, then type into a validateHttp field and watch one line appear at the bottom of a five-layer stack. For the usage side of Signal Forms, Part 1 through Part 4 of the series cover the API from the outside. This one was the floor beneath it. If you found this helpful, follow me here and on LinkedIn for more deep dives into Angular, web performance, and modern frontend development. I also send the longer, more opinionated version of this kind of thing to a small list — reading the source, and what it changes about how you build. Subscribe here . See you in the next one! 🤙🏻 — G.
items.summary_html:
Let's be honest: async validation is the part of any forms library where you brace yourself. Debouncing, cancelling the request the user just invalidated by typing another character, keeping a "checking..." spinner honest, not letting a slow response overwrite a fast one. Every library that has ever done this has grown a pile of bespoke machinery for it.

So when Signal Forms shipped validateHttp() and it just worked, I wanted to see the pile. I opened the source expecting a few hundred lines of async bookkeeping, and instead found a function whose entire body is a single call to something else.

That turned into a trace all the way down, from a form field to the line where bytes actually leave the browser. Six layers, and only two of them add anything you could call new async machinery.

✅ Availability: validateHttp() is @publicApi 22.0, stable. Every source reference in this article is pinned to the v22.1.1 tag, so the line numbers stay valid even as main moves.

🧩 The View From Outside

The usage is unremarkable, which is the point. You declare that a field validates against an endpoint, and you're done:

const schema = form(this.model, (path) => {
  validateHttp(path.username, {
    request: ({ value }) => `/api/username-available?u=${value()}`,
    debounce: 300,
    onError: () => ({ kind: 'server-unreachable' }),
    onSuccess: (res: { available: boolean }) =>
      res.available ? undefined : { kind: 'username-taken' },
  });
});

Sync validators run first, the request waits until they pass, field().pending() is true while it's in flight, and typing again cancels the previous call. If you've read Part 3 of my Signal Forms series, that's the behaviour contract you already know. The question here is who implements it.

🔍 Layer 1: validateHttp() Is a Delegation

Here is the whole function, from validate_http.ts:

export function validateHttp(path, opts) {
  validateAsync(path, {
    params: opts.request,
    debounce: opts.debounce,
    factory: (request) => httpResource(request, opts.options),
    onSuccess: opts.onSuccess,
    onError: opts.onError,
    when: opts.when,
  });
}

That's it. No await, no subscription, no cancellation logic. The URL function you wrote becomes the params of something, and httpResource() gets handed over as a factory. Out of the whole file, that factory is the only line that does anything HTTP-related; everything else naming HTTP is an import, a type or a doc comment.

So the async machinery is in validateAsync. Let's go there.

🧠 Layer 2: Three Behaviours, Zero New Mechanisms

validate_async.ts is where I expected the pile to be. It isn't there either. Three behaviours, each one built from something that already existed.

Sync-before-async gating is just returning undefined. The computation that feeds the resource's params does this:

if (validationState.shouldSkipValidation() || !validationState.syncValid()) {
  return undefined;
}

A resource() whose params computation returns undefined sits in idle and never calls its loader — loadEffect() returns early as soon as it sees extRequest.request === undefined. That's documented public behaviour, not a forms detail. The docs promise that async validation runs only after all synchronous validation passes. Nobody implemented that promise here. It falls out of a rule that was already there.

pending() is a resource status, read through a validator. The async error rule is a switch (lightly condensed here — the real one wraps each result in addDefaultField() to attach it to the field):

switch (res.status()) {
  case 'idle':                      return undefined;
  case 'loading': case 'reloading': return 'pending';
  case 'resolved': case 'local':
    return res.hasValue() ? opts.onSuccess(res.value()!, ctx) : undefined;
  case 'error':                     return opts.onError(res.error(), ctx);
}

Six resource statuses collapse into four form outcomes. field().pending() holds no state of its own, it's a projection of res.status().

Debounce composes two existing primitives instead of writing a timer:

if (opts.debounce !== undefined) {
  const debouncedResource = debounced(() => params(), opts.debounce);
  const wrappedParams = computed(() => ɵchain(debouncedResource));
  return opts.factory(wrappedParams);
}

debounced() is a public (still experimental) @angular/core primitive, and ɵchain is the internal side of ctx.chain(), the resource-composition helper you reach through a params context. The file does declare export function chain(), but it carries no @publicApi marker and is not surfaced on @angular/core's public entry point, which is why the forms code reaches it through the ɵ-prefixed alias rather than importing it by name. The forms team is chaining a debounced resource into a loader's params exactly the way you would chain any two resources in your own code. Worth noticing that they're dogfooding an experimental API in a stable feature.

⚙️ Layer 3: httpResource() Swaps the Loader

httpResource() extends ResourceImpl and doesn't override any of the loading logic. It passes in a loader that subscribes to HttpClient, and it adds three signals:

Signal What it is Resets on request change? progress linkedSignal sourced from extRequest Yes, by the graph statusCode linkedSignal sourced from extRequest Yes, by the graph headers computed over a linkedSignal, gated on status Yes, plus stays undefined until resolved/error

So changing the request resets all three with no reset code involved — and the gate on headers means you never read half-populated headers mid-flight.

The one place a reset is written by hand is override set(), which clears all three when you write a value locally. The signal graph covers the request path; the local-write path doesn't go through it.

One line inside that loader is the bridge between the signal world and the HTTP world:

sub = this.client.request(request!).subscribe({ /* ... */ });
🔧 Layer 4: The Pipeline Everything Shares

ResourceImpl is the actual engine, and it's four reactive nodes. The one I'd single out is the state machine, because it explains a UI behaviour you've probably relied on without asking why:

// the branch taken when the resource already has previous state
status = request === undefined ? 'idle' : 'loading';

There are two of these, one per branch of an if/else inside that linkedSignal. The first covers initialisation and can also resolve straight from an initial stream; the second is the one above, taken when params change on a resource that already exists. Both send undefined to 'idle'. That expression runs inside a linkedSignal, which means it's not behind an await. linkedSignal is lazy, it recomputes on read rather than on write, but that recomputation is pure and synchronous: the first read of status() after your params change already returns 'loading', and pending() is already true, in the same tick, before any promise exists. Only the data is async. If you've ever wondered why Signal Forms' pending state doesn't flicker, that's the reason: the state transition doesn't live inside the async function.

The loader itself is called by exactly one effect whose only tracked dependency is the request. Nobody calls the loader imperatively. The graph decides that work should happen, and a single effect does it. It's the same lazy, pull-based model I traced in Internals #1, which is a good sign: you learn this machine once and it keeps showing up.

🔌 Layer 5: Where the Trace Goes Dark

Follow client.request(...) downward and you hit a wall. HttpClient hands off to HttpHandler, HttpHandler hands off to HttpBackend, and both of those are abstract classes with a single handle() method and no implementation. Grep as hard as you like, no import leads to the code that touches the network.

That's because the binding isn't an import, it's a provider. From provider.ts, reformatted here to fit the width (the real HttpBackend entry uses a block-bodied factory, and each object sits on its own lines):

const providers: Provider[] = [
  HttpClient,
  FetchBackend,
  HttpInterceptorHandler,
  {provide: HttpHandler, useExisting: HttpInterceptorHandler},
  {provide: HttpBackend, useFactory: () => inject(FetchBackend)},
  {provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTOR_FNS, useValue: xsrfInterceptorFn, multi: true},
];

provideHttpClient() is the only place in the framework where those two abstract tokens get a concrete answer. Two details are easy to get wrong here. First, HttpClient itself is @Injectable({providedIn: 'root'}) and FetchBackend is auto-provided too, so both classes are reachable from a bare injector. Forgetting provideHttpClient() doesn't fail on HttpClient, it fails with No provider for HttpHandler, because the class resolves and its dependency doesn't. Second, re-listing HttpClient and the backends in that array isn't redundant. It re-provides them at the environment injector where you called the function. That's what lets a lazy route have its own interceptors, instead of everything collapsing onto one root instance.

This is also why swapping the transport is a one-line change:

Feature What it adds Status at v22.1.1 withFetch() {provide: HttpBackend, useExisting: FetchBackend} Deprecated — "FetchBackend is the default HttpBackend" withXhr() {provide: HttpBackend, useExisting: HttpXhrBackend} Supported — still needed for upload progress and JSONP
🌐 Layer 6: The Floor

FetchBackend is where Angular stops and the platform starts:

private readonly fetchImpl =
  inject(FetchFactory, {optional: true})?.fetch ?? ((...args) => globalThis.fetch(...args));

const fetchPromise = this.ngZone.runOutsideAngular(() =>
  this.fetchImpl(request.urlWithParams, {signal, ...init}),
);

Even the last hop is injectable. And notice handle() returns new Observable(...), so nothing was sent until layer 3 called .subscribe(). The cold Observable is the hinge the whole chain turns on: the resource's effect decides when, and the subscription is the trigger.

Cancellation runs back up the same path in reverse. Typing another character changes the params signal, so the effect aborts its AbortController, the httpResource loader unsubscribes, the RxJS teardown aborts a second AbortController inside FetchBackend, and that one is the signal handed to fetch. Four different cancellation idioms relayed in sequence, with a staleness check at the top that rejects a late response by object identity in case anything slips through.

✅ Closing Thoughts

Lined up, the whole stack is one pipeline with one part swapped at each level:

Layer What it swaps What it adds validateHttp() The params Nothing at all — the body is one delegating call validateAsync() The params again, now gated and debounced The translation from resource status into form errors httpResource() The loader headers(), statusCode(), progress() ResourceImpl Nothing — it is the pipeline Status, cancellation, staleness HttpClient The transport, through DI Interceptors, XSRF, the transfer cache FetchBackend Nothing either — it's the floor Chunked body reading, progress, timeouts, and finally globalThis.fetch

FetchBackend is the one row worth a caveat: there is real code down there, it just isn't async validation code. None of the debouncing, cancelling or pending-state logic we came looking for lives below ResourceImpl.

The reason this matters beyond trivia: there's no forms-specific async system to learn, work around, or wait on the team to extend. If you understand resource(), you already understand validateHttp(), and anything it does you can reproduce with public APIs. Gate a loader by returning undefined. Render pending state off status(). Debounce by chaining a debounced() resource into your params. That's the entire feature.

It's also a fair signal about the abstraction's honesty. A thin layer over primitives you can reach yourself is one you can debug at 6pm on a Friday, and one that inherits every improvement made underneath it for free.

If you want to walk it yourself, clone the repo at v22.1.1 and read in this order: validate_http.ts, validate_async.ts, common/http/src/resource.ts, then core/src/resource/resource.ts (the constructor, then loadEffect). A nice runtime check: provide a custom FetchFactory that logs, then type into a validateHttp field and watch one line appear at the bottom of a five-layer stack.

For the usage side of Signal Forms, Part 1 through Part 4 of the series cover the API from the outside. This one was the floor beneath it.

If you found this helpful, follow me here and on LinkedIn for more deep dives into Angular, web performance, and modern frontend development.

I also send the longer, more opinionated version of this kind of thing to a small list — reading the source, and what it changes about how you build. Subscribe here.

See you in the next one! 🤙🏻
— G.

items.title: He left OpenAI to become a filmmaker. He said AI coding was 'lonelier' and 'mentally draining.'
items.summary: Former OpenAI employee Kasra Kyanzadeh said that AI coding made him "miss people." Kasra Kyanzadeh Kasra Kyanzadeh worked at OpenAI for two months. He said he worried that AI coding had "gone too far." He told Business Insider that AI agents let a single software engineer own a project. That reality made him lonely. "You don't get that same feeling of: We accomplished this thing together," he said. Kasra Kyanzadeh missed working with people. "I was like: Where are there smart people?" the 33-year-old engineer told Business Insider. "At OpenAI, there are smart people." So, Kyanzadeh joined the team building the Codex desktop app in June. By mid-August, he said he was feeling tired and drained. He left to pursue filmmaking. It wasn't OpenAI that was the problem, he said. It was coding with AI agents. Kyanzadeh is one of many engineers who have expressed fatigue with AI coding tools. As AI transforms the job of a software engineer, some developers aren't happy with their new roles. He had enough money to support a career change. Kyanzadeh joined Airtable when it had five employees and later joined Watershed when it was small, too. After Watershed, he founded Lightpage, an AI notebook app. This was 2024, the era of "tab completion models," which he looks back on fondly. "That removed a lot of the annoying boilerplate of writing syntax, but we were still thinking about the code and the architecture," he said. In December, coding "slipped," he said. One person can own an entire feature with their AI agents , he said, so there's less collaboration among engineers. This is me I ended up leaving OpenAI, not because there's anything wrong with OAI (I actually think they're underrated as a biz), but because to me, building commercial software doesn't feel fun anymore Because agents write ~all the code: - There’s less human to human… https://t.co/DYyqG3jvi3 — Kasra (@kasrak) August 25, 2026 When he was younger, Kyanzadeh loved having a whole project to himself, mapping it all out in his head. "Maybe it's gone too far," he said. "I miss people." The lonely AI coders There were other ways to find community at OpenAI. Kyanzadeh praised OpenAI's employees and said the company had "all the usual stuff," like happy hours. But it doesn't "scratch the same itch," he said, when the day-to-day work is one-person projects. "Human bonding happens best through stress," he said. "When every person is working on their own project, you don't get that same feeling of: We accomplished this thing together." He also struggled to get into a flow state , he said. Each task takes a few minutes, which he called "the worst amount of time." It's not enough time to do something meaningful, he said, but it's enough time you'll want to perform another task. So, Kyanzadeh would set up another agent. "Now you're juggling five, six different threads," he said. "Or, you open Twitter." Then there's the time spent reviewing the code and checking for errors. "Most people have never liked code review," Kyanzadeh said. "It was always just a thing we had to do. But, as a percentage of time, it has grown." The result is fatiguing , he said. He's not alone. Some developers told Business Insider that AI caused workplace paralysis . Anthropic engineering leader Fiona Fung said AI agents made the company's programmers lonelier. So, Kyanzadeh decided to leave. He's always wanted to try filmmaking and decided to get out of commercial software. The team was kind about it, he said, and he finished the project he was working on before he left. "To me, OpenAI was an experiment of: What is it like to build software on a large scale in this new era?" he said. "It turned out, I don't feel like I'm doing my best work anymore." Are you a software engineer who recently pivoted careers? Reach out to the reporter at hchandonnet@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

Former OpenAI employee Kasra Kyanzadeh said that AI coding made him "miss people."

Kasra Kyanzadeh

  • Kasra Kyanzadeh worked at OpenAI for two months. He said he worried that AI coding had "gone too far."
  • He told Business Insider that AI agents let a single software engineer own a project. That reality made him lonely.
  • "You don't get that same feeling of: We accomplished this thing together," he said.

Kasra Kyanzadeh missed working with people.

"I was like: Where are there smart people?" the 33-year-old engineer told Business Insider. "At OpenAI, there are smart people."

So, Kyanzadeh joined the team building the Codex desktop app in June. By mid-August, he said he was feeling tired and drained. He left to pursue filmmaking.

It wasn't OpenAI that was the problem, he said. It was coding with AI agents.

Kyanzadeh is one of many engineers who have expressed fatigue with AI coding tools. As AI transforms the job of a software engineer, some developers aren't happy with their new roles.

He had enough money to support a career change. Kyanzadeh joined Airtable when it had five employees and later joined Watershed when it was small, too. After Watershed, he founded Lightpage, an AI notebook app. This was 2024, the era of "tab completion models," which he looks back on fondly.

"That removed a lot of the annoying boilerplate of writing syntax, but we were still thinking about the code and the architecture," he said.

In December, coding "slipped," he said. One person can own an entire feature with their AI agents, he said, so there's less collaboration among engineers.

This is me

I ended up leaving OpenAI, not because there's anything wrong with OAI (I actually think they're underrated as a biz), but because to me, building commercial software doesn't feel fun anymore

Because agents write ~all the code:
- There’s less human to human… https://t.co/DYyqG3jvi3

— Kasra (@kasrak) August 25, 2026

When he was younger, Kyanzadeh loved having a whole project to himself, mapping it all out in his head.

"Maybe it's gone too far," he said. "I miss people."

The lonely AI coders

There were other ways to find community at OpenAI. Kyanzadeh praised OpenAI's employees and said the company had "all the usual stuff," like happy hours.

But it doesn't "scratch the same itch," he said, when the day-to-day work is one-person projects.

"Human bonding happens best through stress," he said. "When every person is working on their own project, you don't get that same feeling of: We accomplished this thing together."

He also struggled to get into a flow state, he said. Each task takes a few minutes, which he called "the worst amount of time." It's not enough time to do something meaningful, he said, but it's enough time you'll want to perform another task.

So, Kyanzadeh would set up another agent. "Now you're juggling five, six different threads," he said. "Or, you open Twitter."

Then there's the time spent reviewing the code and checking for errors.

"Most people have never liked code review," Kyanzadeh said. "It was always just a thing we had to do. But, as a percentage of time, it has grown."

The result is fatiguing, he said.

He's not alone. Some developers told Business Insider that AI caused workplace paralysis. Anthropic engineering leader Fiona Fung said AI agents made the company's programmers lonelier.

So, Kyanzadeh decided to leave. He's always wanted to try filmmaking and decided to get out of commercial software. The team was kind about it, he said, and he finished the project he was working on before he left.

"To me, OpenAI was an experiment of: What is it like to build software on a large scale in this new era?" he said. "It turned out, I don't feel like I'm doing my best work anymore."

items.title: I worked 13-hour days building my startup while working at Apple. Here's why I ignored advice to go all in sooner.
items.summary: Julie Zhu built her startup before and after work while she was still employed at Apple. Julie Zhu Julie Zhu spent eight months building her startup while working full time at Apple. She structured her days around both jobs, often working about 13 hours. She waited to quit until she felt financially secure and confident in her business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Julie Zhu, a 29-year-old entrepreneur in New York City who left Apple last year to focus on her startup, Odd One In. The following has been edited for length and clarity. A few years ago, I started considering leaving my job at Apple and making the leap into entrepreneurship. A lot of people around me thought the decision was obvious: I should just quit. There were a few factors nudging me out the door. For one, I had wanted to become a founder since I was 18. I'd also developed a sort of love-hate relationship with Apple, where I began working in 2022. I was grateful for what I learned there, but I felt like it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment — and I also struggled with imposter syndrome. I wanted to build something where I had more of a say and could make more decisions. When I sought advice from people I knew, including those in the startup community, about 95% told me, "Julie, if you're not happy at Apple, you should just quit." They said I had the perfect résumé and that venture capital firms would likely be willing to give me money — or at least talk to me. They thought it was fine that I hadn't fully figured out my business idea yet. I realized I didn't have to follow the path that worked for other people. I wanted to chart my own. Quitting before I felt prepared wasn't the right decision for me. Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations. Share your story by filling out this form . I wanted a plan before I quit I think a lot of people who told me to quit gave me that advice because they'd found success in the startup world , which made it easier for them to tell me to take the risk. The truth is no one knows what it's like to walk in your shoes — or what decision is right for you. For me, completing a checklist I'd given myself before leaving Apple was really important. That included having a tangible idea I believed in, a team, and enough of a foundation to feel like I wasn't jumping completely blind. Financial security mattered a lot. I wanted to make sure I had about three to five years of runway across my assets and savings, including my Apple stock. I also wanted my family's support. My parents are entrepreneurs, and I wanted them to understand why I was giving up a comfortable corporate job, particularly when layoffs were happening across the tech industry. As I reflected on the best course of action, I talked everything through with my therapist. I wanted to be rational and logical about my decision. Julie Zhu waited to leave Apple until she felt confident about her startup's trajectory and her financial security. Julie Zhu My business idea started coming together By late 2024, some of those pieces were starting to come together. I found a cofounder who was already a friend of mine. Having that existing friendship and trust made it much easier for us to start building something together. From there, we started developing an idea I'd had for Odd One In, an artist collectible company. We officially started the business in December 2024, but I wasn't ready to leave Apple. So I decided to do both. Before incorporating Odd One In, I checked with Apple's business conduct team to make sure I could work on my company while employed there, and started building it outside my Apple work hours. For the next eight months, that meant structuring nearly my entire day around my two jobs. I built my startup before and after work While building my startup and working full-time at Apple, I would wake up around 5:30 a.m. and go to the gym — usually doing some cardio to wake myself up and stay healthy. Then I'd work on Odd One In from around 6 to 8 a.m. After that, I'd head to Apple for my day job. I'd typically get home around 5 p.m., eat, and start working on the startup again. I'd often work until around 10:30 p.m., then go to sleep and do it all over again the next day. On a typical weekday, I was spending roughly 13 to 14 hours working across Apple and the startup. It was a demanding schedule, but I had a plan for my business with specific milestones I wanted to achieve. That made the extra work feel intentional, rather than like I was just "working all the time." I finally felt ready to go all in and quit my job By August 2025, juggling both my Apple job and Odd One In had become too much, in part because my business was demanding more of my time. I also didn't think continuing was fair to my team at Apple . I'd found something I was more passionate about, and many of the pieces I'd wanted in place before quitting had come together. This included getting my parents' support for my decision to leave Apple. It took time for them to understand why the move was important to me, but once they understood my reasoning and saw real traction from what we were building, they became much more supportive. Overall, I finally felt confident that after four years with the company, it was the right time to move on. I'm glad I didn't quit before I was comfortable Since leaving, being a founder has been humbling, but it's also given me confidence. At Apple, I sometimes felt like a small part of a huge company. Building something from zero to one has shown me I'm capable of doing much more. Odd One In generated close to six figures in annual revenue last year, but I'm not paying myself a salary yet because we're reinvesting the money to grow the business, including production, warehousing, paying artists, and other expenses. We're completely bootstrapped: We haven't raised any outside funding and launched with our own savings. To pay my personal expenses, I've relied on the savings I accumulated while working at Apple and earlier in my career. Looking back, I'm glad I didn't follow the advice to quit before I was comfortable. There's a romanticized idea in the startup world that you have to take the leap and figure everything out afterward. That can work for some people. For me, spending eight months doing both made me feel confident in my decision to go all in. Do you have a story to share? items.summary_html:
Julie Zhu built her startup before and after work while she was still employed at Apple.

Julie Zhu

  • Julie Zhu spent eight months building her startup while working full time at Apple.
  • She structured her days around both jobs, often working about 13 hours.
  • She waited to quit until she felt financially secure and confident in her business.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Julie Zhu, a 29-year-old entrepreneur in New York City who left Apple last year to focus on her startup, Odd One In. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

A few years ago, I started considering leaving my job at Apple and making the leap into entrepreneurship. A lot of people around me thought the decision was obvious: I should just quit.

There were a few factors nudging me out the door. For one, I had wanted to become a founder since I was 18. I'd also developed a sort of love-hate relationship with Apple, where I began working in 2022.

I was grateful for what I learned there, but I felt like it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment — and I also struggled with imposter syndrome. I wanted to build something where I had more of a say and could make more decisions.

When I sought advice from people I knew, including those in the startup community, about 95% told me, "Julie, if you're not happy at Apple, you should just quit."

They said I had the perfect résumé and that venture capital firms would likely be willing to give me money — or at least talk to me. They thought it was fine that I hadn't fully figured out my business idea yet.

I realized I didn't have to follow the path that worked for other people. I wanted to chart my own. Quitting before I felt prepared wasn't the right decision for me.

Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

I wanted a plan before I quit

I think a lot of people who told me to quit gave me that advice because they'd found success in the startup world, which made it easier for them to tell me to take the risk.

The truth is no one knows what it's like to walk in your shoes — or what decision is right for you.

For me, completing a checklist I'd given myself before leaving Apple was really important. That included having a tangible idea I believed in, a team, and enough of a foundation to feel like I wasn't jumping completely blind.

Financial security mattered a lot. I wanted to make sure I had about three to five years of runway across my assets and savings, including my Apple stock.

I also wanted my family's support. My parents are entrepreneurs, and I wanted them to understand why I was giving up a comfortable corporate job, particularly when layoffs were happening across the tech industry.

As I reflected on the best course of action, I talked everything through with my therapist. I wanted to be rational and logical about my decision.

Julie Zhu waited to leave Apple until she felt confident about her startup's trajectory and her financial security.

Julie Zhu

My business idea started coming together

By late 2024, some of those pieces were starting to come together. I found a cofounder who was already a friend of mine. Having that existing friendship and trust made it much easier for us to start building something together.

From there, we started developing an idea I'd had for Odd One In, an artist collectible company. We officially started the business in December 2024, but I wasn't ready to leave Apple. So I decided to do both.

Before incorporating Odd One In, I checked with Apple's business conduct team to make sure I could work on my company while employed there, and started building it outside my Apple work hours.

For the next eight months, that meant structuring nearly my entire day around my two jobs.

I built my startup before and after work

While building my startup and working full-time at Apple, I would wake up around 5:30 a.m. and go to the gym — usually doing some cardio to wake myself up and stay healthy. Then I'd work on Odd One In from around 6 to 8 a.m.

After that, I'd head to Apple for my day job. I'd typically get home around 5 p.m., eat, and start working on the startup again. I'd often work until around 10:30 p.m., then go to sleep and do it all over again the next day. On a typical weekday, I was spending roughly 13 to 14 hours working across Apple and the startup.

It was a demanding schedule, but I had a plan for my business with specific milestones I wanted to achieve. That made the extra work feel intentional, rather than like I was just "working all the time."

I finally felt ready to go all in and quit my job

By August 2025, juggling both my Apple job and Odd One In had become too much, in part because my business was demanding more of my time.

I also didn't think continuing was fair to my team at Apple. I'd found something I was more passionate about, and many of the pieces I'd wanted in place before quitting had come together.

This included getting my parents' support for my decision to leave Apple. It took time for them to understand why the move was important to me, but once they understood my reasoning and saw real traction from what we were building, they became much more supportive.

Overall, I finally felt confident that after four years with the company, it was the right time to move on.

I'm glad I didn't quit before I was comfortable

Since leaving, being a founder has been humbling, but it's also given me confidence. At Apple, I sometimes felt like a small part of a huge company. Building something from zero to one has shown me I'm capable of doing much more.

Odd One In generated close to six figures in annual revenue last year, but I'm not paying myself a salary yet because we're reinvesting the money to grow the business, including production, warehousing, paying artists, and other expenses. We're completely bootstrapped: We haven't raised any outside funding and launched with our own savings. To pay my personal expenses, I've relied on the savings I accumulated while working at Apple and earlier in my career.

Looking back, I'm glad I didn't follow the advice to quit before I was comfortable. There's a romanticized idea in the startup world that you have to take the leap and figure everything out afterward. That can work for some people.

For me, spending eight months doing both made me feel confident in my decision to go all in.

items.title: I'm the CEO of Oura. I wake up at 5 a.m. when things are going well, and 3:30 a.m. when they're not. Here's what a day in my life looks like.
items.summary: Jason Henry for BI This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tom Hale, the 57-year-old CEO of Oura Health , based in San Francisco. It's been edited for length and clarity. I became the CEO of Oura in March 2022. We make the Oura Ring , a smart ring that delivers personalized health data and insights to help people live more balanced lives. My career spans more than 30 years in technology and consumer products, including serving as president of SurveyMonkey . Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. Here's what a typical day in my life in San Francisco looks like. 5 a.m. — No alarm necessary I wake up around 5 a.m. every day without an alarm. The first thing I do is check my Oura Ring. items.title: How decoding beluga whales’ chitchat may save them – and teach us more about ourselves
items.summary: From humpbacks learning the latest songs to sperm whales’ ‘clan codas’, drones and AI learning are helping reveal another dimension to the concept of culture In 2015, the whale researcher Valeria Vergara pitched a small tent at the icy water’s edge on Somerset Island in the remote Canadian high Arctic, shrouded in a freezing fog so thick she struggled to see her own hands. She trailed a cord out to the coast and plopped a hydrophone into the water to record the calls of belugas. As many as 1,000 of the whales, accompanied by their newborn calves, frequented the surrounding bay. Belugas’ ceaseless chatter, made up of dozens of unique sounds, is crucial to keeping these creatures connected in the dim, turbid waters of the Arctic. Continue reading...

items.title: Everyone hates performative LinkedIn posts. Workers feel like they have to write them anyway.
items.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI Many workers feel they need to build a personal brand on LinkedIn to get ahead. Some companies are even paying ghostwriters to create LinkedIn posts for their employees. The posting arms race has also fueled performative content, oversharing, and AI slop. Workers on LinkedIn are finding themselves in a catch-22: They may cringe at the self-promotional, carefully polished posts that fill their feeds, but still believe they need to build a personal brand of their own. Some companies are even stepping in to post for them. Corporate ghostwriting firm Hat Tip creates LinkedIn posts for founders and, increasingly, their employees. Founder Christian Di Bratto calls it a sales and marketing strategy for a world where brands may be losing their appeal. He recently quoted a client $8,400 a month to write LinkedIn posts for three employees, three times a week. "People want to buy from people," Di Bratto said. "This employee portion of it is the next evolution of what founder-led content was. With the rise of grindslop and the migration away from X, LinkedIn is now a hybrid of performative professional posting and personal sharing. Many workers view posting there as a necessary career investment , made easier by the rise of AI tools. Even LinkedIn is rethinking all this posting. In July, the company started letting users flag posts that seem "like AI slop." Pangram, an AI-detection firm, estimated that 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts and 30% of shorter posts it analyzed between April and June were likely AI-generated . LinkedIn says its recent changes have reduced the amount of AI slop on the platform. Why workers feel like they need to post so much on LinkedIn When a former Microsoft manager was laid off last year, he began regularly posting on LinkedIn about his field. After seeing recruiters and career coaches online emphasize the importance of building a personal brand on the platform, it felt like something he couldn't afford not to try. "We all have to be content creators on top of our actual jobs — or lack of jobs — and perform being a candidate," he said. It's not just struggling job seekers who've come to view regular LinkedIn posting as a key part of managing their careers. Muskan Agarwal, who is based in India and runs Cherry Media, a marketing agency that helps professionals and creators grow their online presence, said she's seen a surge in tech workers looking to build personal brands on platforms like LinkedIn. Her clients include current and former US-based employees of companies including Microsoft, Amazon, and Google. Agarwal said some aren't trying to become full-time creators, and that their goals include landing better jobs, speaking opportunities, or professional connections. Each client, she said, pays her agency for at least three months of services. Do you have a story to share about posting on LinkedIn? Reach out to these reporters at jzinkula@businessinsider.com and jkaplan@businessinsider.com . Does posting on LinkedIn actually help your career? The million-dollar question for job seekers and workers alike is how much all that posting actually helps their careers. Matt Stabile, founder of the recruiting firm Stabile Search, believes LinkedIn posts have shifted toward engagement-driven content. "The quality has skewed towards 'AI slop' rather than meaningful discussions," he said. Stabile believes posting and attracting engagement can increase someone's visibility on LinkedIn and help establish them as a thought leader, but that posting too much could send the wrong signal to recruiters. "I would say that overposting would be a red flag. If you are busy, in demand and talented, why would you spend your time posting on LinkedIn?" Jason Baxter, the owner and operator of a boutique marketing agency, posts one to two times a week and comments on posts at least ten times a week. He's gotten legitimate business and connections from the platform. Even so, he thinks that over half of the people on LinkedIn are just "out there shouting at the world and not reading what anyone else is saying." How to post without overdoing it Jansel Murad, a vice president at Dukas Linden Public Relations, a financial PR firm, generally recommends clients share one to two posts a week. "If you don't have something authentic to say, hold back, it's okay," Murad said. "Because then you'll probably get further engagement from your network when they see you really sharing updates that matter to you." And even if your authentic voice — which Murad said often seems to hit a sweet spot for the LinkedIn algorithm — wants to be out there five times a week, she would still say to hold back on that rapidity of posting. Instead, maybe bundle posts together. Ultimately, then, the best practice might just be a balance — and, sometimes, leaning into the cringe. Benjamin Chipman, a 25-year-old marketer and content creator who loves posting on LinkedIn, bristles at the concept of a performative poster. Chipman found posting on the platform life-changing during college, and says LinkedIn has been responsible for the majority of his career trajectory. "I don't care if you're posting on Instagram, on LinkedIn, on Facebook, there's a performance element to it all, but it doesn't mean it's inherently not productive," Chipman said. "Those two things can be true at the same time." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The chips powering AI can take years to design. This startup says AI did it in 2 weeks.
items.summary: Architect Labs cofounders Ebrahim Hussain and Aaditya Subedi. Bonnie Rae Mills The startup Architect Labs says it used AI to design and verify a chip in two weeks. An AI model running on the chip then found ways to improve it, its 20-year-old cofounder said. Researchers called the speed impressive, though they said manufacturing will be the ultimate test. AI is coming for one of the hardest jobs in the technology industry: chip design . The nascent startup Architect Labs, founded last year, is betting on the promise of using AI to accelerate design for both chipmakers and companies seeking custom hardware. It says it designed and verified a chip called Redwood in two weeks, with two human chip architects setting and refining the overall plan while AI handled the detailed design work. It would dramatically speed up a process that typically takes a year or more, costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and requires large, specialized teams of around 100 people, the company said. This lengthy timeline is especially problematic in AI, where models evolve faster than the chips they run on, said Architect Labs cofounder and CEO Ebrahim Hussain, who is 20. Architect emerged from stealth in June with a $24 million seed round led by Kindred Ventures. Google's former chief scientist, Jeff Dean, and other executives from OpenAI and Nvidia also backed the startup. Hao Zheng, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Central Florida, called the Redwood timeline "impressive," though he said several startups and more established companies, such as Synopsys, also use AI to accelerate the chip design process. The Redwood experiment revealed something else, said Hussain. After running an AI model on Redwood, the model found ways to improve the chip itself, which he said suggests a self-reinforcing loop. "It's still very early, but we're very excited about the possibility of growing to larger models and getting AI to essentially recursively improve itself and build better and better hardware," Hussain said. Redwood can run AI models like Meta's Llama and Alibaba's Qwen, Architect said, though there's a caveat — it hasn't been manufactured yet. Instead, the design has been tested on reprogrammable hardware known as a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), and Architect said those tests suggest the finished product could be more efficient than Nvidia's Jetson Orin Nano , an AI supercomputer used in robotics. Hussain said the company plans to send Redwood to the Taiwanese chip manufacturer TSMC to be manufactured and hasn't decided when because its AI is still working to improve the design. Manufacturing is the real test, said Zheng, and it will ultimately reveal how fast, efficient, and reliable the chip is. Matthew Guthaus, a computer science and engineering professor at UC Santa Cruz, said that while AI is already good at many parts of chip design, "it can also make silly mistakes and needs close supervision and double-checking." These errors can cost millions if they aren't caught before manufacturing, Guthaus said. Hussain said that Architect's AI system checks its own work for mistakes rather than relying on humans to do so. Hussain said that AI could usher in a new era for the chip industry. While TSMC helped introduce a "fabless" era, allowing companies like Nvidia to design chips without owning factories, he says the next phase will be "designless" — putting custom chips within reach without the huge teams traditionally required to build them. items.title: Sam Altman knows people hate data centers
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has acknowledged the headwinds the AI industry is facing. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman knows people don't love AI right now. Altman told Time Magazine that "Clearly, people hate data centers—right now, at least." In the US, the AI industry is facing significant headwinds, especially in data center construction. Sam Altman doesn't need to see the polls . The OpenAI CEO knows how unpopular his industry has become. "Clearly, people hate data centers—right now, at least," Altman told Time as part of a series of interviews for a cover story published on Wednesday. "People are pretty negative on AI." Data centers in particular have become quite the pariah. Altman has previously spoken about the backlash against the industry, including local opposition to data center projects nationwide. "I understand emotionally why people don't want data centers in their backyard in the same way that I don't really want a nuclear power plant next to my house, even though I know it's a super safe thing," Altman said during an interview last month. In March, Altman was blunt in his assessment at a BlackRock event. "AI is not very popular in the US right now," Altman said during BlackRock's US Infrastructure Summit in Washington, D.C. In April, an attacker threw a Molotov cocktail at Altman's San Francisco mansion and later threatened to burn down OpenAI before being taken into custody. "A lot of the criticism of our industry comes from sincere concern about the incredibly high stakes of this technology," Altman wrote in a post on his personal blog after the attack. He added that "overall, I believe technological progress can make the future unbelievably good, for your family and mine. " Some companies, including OpenAI, have taken steps to address some of the biggest flashpoints in the data center debate, including water usage and power consumption. OpenAI has also announced community benefits, including Codex credits for eligible students in Ohio, Georgia, and Michigan, three places where it's building data centers. The backlash has only continued to grow In the last month, governors in Pennsylvania and Texas, both of whom are running for reelection in November, sought to curtail future data center development in their states after previously extolling the benefits of such projects. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, who once said his state was the "epicenter of AI development," said the industry had only itself to blame . "They pop up in places that nobody ever heard of before, until they started the construction," Abbott said on Sunday during an interview on ABC's "This Week". "And so, they had not been working in collaboration with the state, they'd not been in collaboration with local governments, and so they basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them and that's why they got the backlash they deserve." To top it all off, Super Bowl champion Jason Kelce starred in a cheeky ad for his and his brother Travis' beer company, Garage Beer, and canned water brand Liquid Death, where he suggested that people send their pee to data centers — adding a whole new dimension to the phrase "pissed off." Investor Chamath Palihapitiya, co-host of the "All-In Podcast," compared the situation to a "powder keg. " He said, "The safer bet may be that the pushback and resistance grow." "Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy," Palihapitiya wrote in a post on X last week. And even President Donald Trump , who has fashioned himself as a champion of the industry and argued that strict regulations could cost the US in the AI race, recently suggested data centers might benefit from a better message. "I would say that maybe it could use a little public relations help," Trump told reporters at the White House. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Alcohol became a flashpoint in the US-Canada trade war. Now both sides say they're losing.
items.summary: Alcohol makers in the US and Canada say they're hurting as a result of the trade war. John Fedele/Getty Images The US-Canada trade war escalated on Saturday with new 50% tariffs on Canadian alcohol. American booze was pulled from Canadian shelves last year and remains restricted in most of Canada. Alcohol makers in the US and Canada say both industries are hurting. What started as an eye-catching retaliation tactic to tariffs has become a sticking point in the US-Canada trade war — and neither side is standing down. The booze battle began last year after President Donald Trump imposed broad 25% tariffs on Canadian goods. Canada responded with its own 25% retaliatory tariffs targeting alcohol, among other products. The country's provinces went further, pulling American alcohol from shelves and halting new purchases or distribution. A year and a half later, American alcohol remains shut out of much of Canada. The boycott was so effective that Trump cited it as a driving force for his latest tariffs, including a 50% tariff on alcohol from Canada that took effect on Saturday after talks between the two countries broke down. While there's been plenty of finger-pointing about who started what, alcohol industries on both sides of the border say they're losing. "Our industry is really just an unfortunate victim," Chris Swonger, CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, said. "It's been devastating for the US industry over the last year and a half, and it's going to be significantly devastating for the Canadian spirits industry, but it'll trickle down and have an effect all the way from bartenders to our distributor partners to retailers to the American hospitality economy." Alcohol represents just a tiny sliver of the hundreds of billions of dollars in goods traded between the US and Canada, but the impact of the trade war on the industry has been especially severe and visible, in part due to the outright bans as well as the direct impact on beloved alcohol brands. For alcohol makers, the industry is also an unusual target for a trade war that's partially aimed at shifting manufacturing back to the US. Unlike other goods, alcohol is often prized specifically because of its country of origin. You can't make Canadian whisky in the US. "An American consumer may love Canadian whisky, and someone else may love tequila," Swonger said. The US and Canadian industries are calling for an end to the alcohol bans and tariffs Canadian provinces, which control alcohol imports, enacted bans on American alcohol around March 2025, the same month Canada levied its retaliatory tariffs. While those tariffs were lifted in September 2025, most of the province-level bans remained in place. Some provinces started allowing existing American stock to be sold, but continued to ban new imports. Eight out of 10 provinces still have some restrictions in place, with Alberta and Saskatchewan as the exceptions. The bans turned out to be one of the more headline-grabbing results of the trade war. They were also effective at inflicting economic pain: Imports of US alcohol to Canada fell by 81%, from about $718 million to $137 million, from March 2025 through February 2026, compared with the preceding year, according to the White House. In comparison, total US exports to Canada fell 4.8% in 2025. American alcohol makers felt they were being unfairly targeted. Lawson Whiting, CEO of Brown-Forman, the parent company of Jack Daniel's , said last year the bans were a "disproportionate" response to the tariffs. On an earnings call in June, the company said its organic sales in Canada fell nearly 60% in its 2026 fiscal year, as its products remained off shelves in most Canadian provinces. Canadian provinces banned American alcohol in early 2025. Most of those restrictions are still in place. VCG/VCG via Getty Images Now, Canadian makers, which are far more dependent on the US market than their American counterparts are on the Canadian market, face Trump's new 50% tariffs, which he said were a direct response to "Canadian discrimination" against American-made booze. The tariffs impact spirits, wine, and beer, with the most popular Canadian booze export to the US being Canadian whisky . Popular brands like Crown Royal, Canadian Club, and Fireball — the latter of which is made in America with imported Canadian whisky — could be affected. "Both the Canadian and American spirits industries have felt significant impacts of this broader trade dispute," Cal Bricker, President and CEO of Spirits Canada, said in a statement in July. Canadian spirit makers rely more heavily on exports to the US than American makers do on exports to Canada. Before the bans, Canada accounted for about 10% of US spirits exports. But 93% of all of Canada's spirits exports by value went to the US, according to Spirits Canada. Of all the spirits produced in Canada, nearly 50% are tied to US demand, the group says. The bans on American alcohol didn't necessarily translate to an increase in sales for Canadian makers, either. Following the bans, overall spirits sales in Canada fell about 4.4% by volume, while sales volumes of Canadian-made spirits were essentially flat, according to Spirits Canada. The alcohol bans were a key part of the failed negotiations The provincial bans became a major talking point last week as Canadian and US officials sought to make a deal to avoid new tariffs. Swonger said the alcohol industry feels it has unfairly become a "leverage point in broader trade negotiations." He said that while distillers appreciated Trump's efforts to prioritize the US alcohol industry going into negotiations, they also wanted to avoid the new 50% tariffs and get the bans lifted instead. Prime Minister Mark Carney asked Canadian provinces to return US alcohol to their shelves last week as the countries closed in on a deal. Officials in two provinces, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, signaled they were ready to lift bans on American alcohol if a broader deal was reached. Newfoundland said Thursday it would resume ordering American products, but changed course days later after the trade talks failed. Canadian makers have also been telling the Canadian provincial governments that the policy intended to punish America is endangering them as well. "While intended as a response to broader trade tensions, those measures have now become the stated basis for direct US retaliation against Canadian spirits exports," Spirits Canada said in July, encouraging the federal and provincial governments to work together to avoid US retaliation. Now, trade associations in Canada and the US are pushing for the same goal: end the mini trade war over alcohol. "We like to compete by sip and taste," Swonger said. "Not by trade barriers." items.title: What smart people are saying about Meta's settlement
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg arrives to the Los Angeles Superior Court at United States Court House on February 18, 2026. Meta agreed to put greater restrictions on teen users on Wednesday. Jill Connelly/Getty Images Meta settled a teen social media addiction lawsuit with states for about $18 billion. Some experts called the deal shrewd, saying Meta avoided potentially massive damages. Critics say the deal is too weak and its teen protections could prove difficult to enforce. Attorneys and analysts are divided on whether Meta made the right move. The social media giant on Wednesday settled with a group of states that sued the company in 2023 and alleged that it had designed its social media platforms to be addictive to teenagers. Included in the settlement are a slew of restrictions for teen users of Instagram and Facebook. If the federal judge overseeing the case approves the settlement, teen users will be limited to two hours of scrolling per day, will be unable to scroll at night, and won't get notifications during the school day. Also in the settlement is around $18 billion for 47 states, the District of Columbia, and several American territories, to be paid out by Meta in installments over the next decade. Around $5 billion of that sum is contingent upon YouTube and TikTok also coughing up billions and instituting similar controls for teen users. Meta and the attorneys general struck the deal less than two weeks after the trial began. Here's what smart people are saying about Meta's landmark social media settlement. Ari Cohn, First Amendment lawyer Cohn, a First Amendment lawyer in Chicago, called the settlement a "shrewd business move, but awful for free speech." Cohn said that by calling on YouTube and TikTok to institute similar restrictions, Meta is "attempting regulatory capture" by setting a standard it hopes rival social media giants will follow. Uttara Ananthakrishnan, associate professor at the University of Washington Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington, told Business Insider that she wouldn't be surprised if YouTube and TikTok announce similar restrictions in the coming days. Ananthakrishnan, who has authored several research papers about the addictive qualities of TikTok, said that while she welcomed the restrictions announced Wednesday, she doubts they'll live up to expectations. "Meta doesn't have a great reputation of enforcing its own policies," she said. Ananthakrishnan pointed to a teen social media ban in Australia , which has largely failed to keep young users off the platforms, as a reason why it's difficult for companies to verify checks. "Enforcement is going to be really difficult," she said. "A motivated, 16-year-old and 18-year-old will just adopt a VPN, log in from their parents' accounts or whatever." Jonathan Turley, professor at George Washington University Law School Jonathan Turley, a professor at George Washington University Law School, said Meta's monetary payout was a big lowball. "The $16 billion is a bit like monopoly money," Turley wrote on X. "Meta succeeded in tying off the potential for massive damages while making changes that was already moving to incorporate in its platform." Turley added that although the settlement will lead to new protections for children on social media, they will ultimately not last. "The technology is too popular and too accessible to create a true firewall," Turley wrote. "The burden will remain with parents." Jason Kint, CEO of Digital Content Next Jason Kint, who leads Digital Content Next, a trade organization that represents digital media companies, said the case impacts an entire generation of children. "Wow. $16 BILLION means Meta/Facebook/Instagram is now approaching $25 BILLION they've on settlements related to consumer protection abuses," he wrote on X on Wednesday. Gary Marcus, tech researcher and writer Marcus, a tech researcher, wrote on X that he hopes other social media platforms will follow suit with guardrails. "I hope that X, TikTok, and YouTube will match these social media restrictions for teens, including 'Productive Pauses,' 'Nighttime blocks,' limited school-time access for children, tighter content controls, stronger and more straightforward parental controls, and limits on things like beauty filters and visible likes," he wrote on Wednesday. He added, "Adults (me included!) would be wise to opt-in for a lot of the same." Read the original article on Business Insider

Here's what smart people are saying about Meta's landmark social media settlement.

Ari Cohn, First Amendment lawyer

Cohn, a First Amendment lawyer in Chicago, called the settlement a "shrewd business move, but awful for free speech."

Cohn said that by calling on YouTube and TikTok to institute similar restrictions, Meta is "attempting regulatory capture" by setting a standard it hopes rival social media giants will follow.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, associate professor at the University of Washington

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington, told Business Insider that she wouldn't be surprised if YouTube and TikTok announce similar restrictions in the coming days.

Ananthakrishnan, who has authored several research papers about the addictive qualities of TikTok, said that while she welcomed the restrictions announced Wednesday, she doubts they'll live up to expectations.

"Meta doesn't have a great reputation of enforcing its own policies," she said.

Ananthakrishnan pointed to a teen social media ban in Australia, which has largely failed to keep young users off the platforms, as a reason why it's difficult for companies to verify checks.

"Enforcement is going to be really difficult," she said. "A motivated, 16-year-old and 18-year-old will just adopt a VPN, log in from their parents' accounts or whatever."

Jonathan Turley, professor at George Washington University Law School

Jonathan Turley, a professor at George Washington University Law School, said Meta's monetary payout was a big lowball.

"The $16 billion is a bit like monopoly money," Turley wrote on X. "Meta succeeded in tying off the potential for massive damages while making changes that was already moving to incorporate in its platform."

Turley added that although the settlement will lead to new protections for children on social media, they will ultimately not last.

"The technology is too popular and too accessible to create a true firewall," Turley wrote. "The burden will remain with parents."

Jason Kint, CEO of Digital Content Next

Jason Kint, who leads Digital Content Next, a trade organization that represents digital media companies, said the case impacts an entire generation of children.

"Wow. $16 BILLION means Meta/Facebook/Instagram is now approaching $25 BILLION they've on settlements related to consumer protection abuses," he wrote on X on Wednesday.

Gary Marcus, tech researcher and writer

Marcus, a tech researcher, wrote on X that he hopes other social media platforms will follow suit with guardrails.

"I hope that X, TikTok, and YouTube will match these social media restrictions for teens, including 'Productive Pauses,' 'Nighttime blocks,' limited school-time access for children, tighter content controls, stronger and more straightforward parental controls, and limits on things like beauty filters and visible likes," he wrote on Wednesday.

He added, "Adults (me included!) would be wise to opt-in for a lot of the same."

items.title: Tennis star Taylor Fritz says playing video games helps keep his brain 'working well' on the court
items.summary: Tennis star Taylor Fritz said playing "League of Legends" helps him decompress. Mike Lawrence/USTA via Getty Images Tennis star Taylor Fritz said playing video games helps him perform better on the court. He enjoys playing "League of Legends," and said the game helps him sharpen his focus. He had also been playing the game in the lead-up to his 2023 Atlanta Open win, he said. Taylor Fritz , 28, said playing " League of Legends " is as much a part of his tennis routine as sleep and recovery. Speaking to GQ in an interview published on Wednesday, the tennis star said playing video games helps him decompress. "When you're training and traveling, you don't always have the energy — nor even should you be going out and doing stuff. You need that time to do something that's not as active," Fritz said. Fritz said he had also seen studies suggesting that the video game he plays, "League of Legends," can improve focus. Developed by Riot Games, the game pits two teams of five against each other, with the goal of destroying the enemy's base. He added that he's experienced those effects himself. "I've definitely noticed crossover: When I feel like my brain's working well when I'm playing the game, my brain's working well when I'm on the court," Fritz said. In the lead-up to his 2023 Atlanta Open win, Fritz said he had been having a good week playing "League of Legends" too, and felt mentally sharp heading into the tournament. "It's like playing chess with pieces that are almost moving without your control. I could feel that my mind was just working really well, and then I could feel that whole week on the court as well," Fritz said. "It was very obvious to me that my decision-making and focus were elevated that week," he continued. Gaming is one part of Fritz's off-court routine. To stay in top shape, he said he aims to eat 200 grams of protein a day and has a go-to Chipotle order that helps him hit that target without going overboard on calories. "It was a lighter portion of rice, no beans, double chicken, the fajita veggies, and then I would go really light sour cream and cheese," Fritz said, adding that he gets hot salsa on the side. With the demanding travel and match schedule on tour, Fritz said he also has to manage his sleep carefully. He adjusts his bedtime depending on when he is due to play a match. If he knows he'll be playing a match at night, he'll start shifting his body clock a few days beforehand by going to sleep as late as 1 a.m. and waking around late morning or noon. "And I'm just starting to get on this weird sleep cycle to where I will feel very awake and ready to play my match if I'm playing at eight," he said. Fritz has previously spoken about the habits that help him stay healthy and focused on tour. He told Business Insider in 2022 that Chipotle is a regular part of his diet during tournament season. "I think a lot of people don't understand how good it is as a post-workout meal. It's got everything," he said. In 2023, Fritz told Business Insider that he needs to have a high-protein breakfast . "I usually don't eat a lot for breakfast, but I always have protein of some kind. I never start my day without it," Fritz said. Read the original article on Business Insider
